explanations: luna: The section’s j-z-y gloss includes the claim that a parent cannot make up for a child; this verse says no soul will be recompensed for another and no ransom or intercession will be accepted, bounding what wealth or kin can do. | terra: لَا تَجْزِى نَفْسٌ عَن نَّفْسٍ شَيْـًٔا denies that one soul can be enough or compensate for another on the day of judgment.

luna: This repeats the section’s j-z-y idea that one person cannot settle another’s account: no soul can avail another, and ransom will not be accepted on that Day. | terra: The repeated judgment warning again denies that one soul can compensate for another, reinforcing the boundary to every human repayment.

luna: This verse describes giving wealth, despite love of it, to relatives, orphans, the needy, and the traveler, alongside patience in hardship. It makes the section’s alternative to hoarding concrete. | terra: Righteousness includes giving wealth despite loving it to relatives, orphans, the needy, travelers, askers, and captives, making release of valued property the proof of faith.

luna: The section says the roots y-s-r and ‘-s-r can name abundance and lack; in the fasting rule here they mean ease and hardship in observance, showing the same pair in a nonfinancial sense. | terra: God intends ease and does not intend hardship for people; the explicit opposition grounds the section's literal yusr/ʿusr axis.
terra: The answer about what to spend is the surplus beyond need, directly bringing adequacy and excess into the measure of giving.
terra: The good loan is multiplied by God, who also constricts and expands; giving, not hoarding, is placed within the true movement between scarcity and abundance.
terra: Believers must spend from their provision before a day on which trade, friendship, and intercession cannot supply what was withheld.
terra: Spending in God's way is pictured as one seed yielding seven hundred grains, reversing the miser's arithmetic of loss and gain.

luna: The section contrasts withholding with giving that seeks no human repayment; this verse describes spenders who do not follow their gift with reminders or injury, so the recipient is not made indebted to the giver. | terra: Those who spend without following the gift by reminders or injury receive their reward from their Lord, separating giving from a claim upon its recipient.

luna: The section opposes b-kh-l to generosity and glosses ghani as wealth and sufficiency; this verse says kind speech and pardon are better than hurtful charity, then calls Allah al-Ghani, joining generous conduct to true sufficiency. | terra: A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by hurt, and God's being Rich closes a warning against transactional giving.
terra: Charity ruined by reminders and injury is like soil washed from bare rock; outward expenditure proves unable to yield when its motive is false.
terra: Those who spend seeking God's pleasure resemble a firmly rooted garden yielding doubly, the fruitful counter-scene to 2:264's stripped rock.

luna: This verse commands spending from the good things people have earned. The section glosses mal as acquired property and depicts the miser keeping possessions back, so this names what should be released. | terra: Believers must spend good acquired things rather than defective ones they would dislike receiving, and the ayah ends by naming God as Rich and Praiseworthy.

luna: The section names fear of poverty as the pressure behind holding wealth back; this verse explicitly says Satan promises poverty while Allah promises forgiveness and bounty, revealing the competing voices around giving. | terra: Satan's promise of poverty gives the fear behind withheld wealth, while God's promise of forgiveness and bounty exposes that fear as a false measure of sufficiency.

luna: The section says the generous person owes no human a return and gives seeking God’s face. This verse says spending is for oneself and is done seeking Allah’s face; what is spent is repaid fully by God. | terra: Spending is to seek God's face, and whatever good is spent is repaid in full; this matches the giver who seeks no human repayment in 92:19-20.
luna: The verse depicts poor people constrained in God’s way who seem self-sufficient because they do not beg insistently. It complicates the section’s equation of visible abundance with actual need.
terra: God erases usury and causes charities to grow, reversing the apparent financial increase of taking and decrease of giving.

luna: The section glosses the roots of al-yusr and al-‘usr as financial plenty and want; here the debtor is actually in ‘usr and is given time until maysara, with charity better still. This is the clearest lived case of the section’s purse moving from shortage toward abundance. | terra: عُسْرَةٍ and مَيْسَرَةٍ stage the section's two roots as a debtor's financial constriction and restored means, while forgiving the debt reverses the miser's withholding.

luna: After 2:280 allows time for a debtor in hardship and recommends charity, this neighboring verse warns of the Day when every soul is repaid in full. Its contribution is the final accounting that makes present wealth and generosity matter.

luna: This verse says wealth and children will not avail the disbelievers against God and that they face the Fire, echoing the section’s boundary on material sufficiency. | terra: لَن تُغْنِيَ عَنْهُمْ أَمْوَالُهُمْ وَلَا أَوْلَادُهُم makes wealth and children unable to avail against God and places their owners at the fire.
terra: Even an earthful of gold offered as ransom is not accepted from one who dies rejecting faith, setting an absolute limit on wealth as compensation.

luna: The section contrasts holding wealth with giving for God’s sake; this verse says righteousness is not attained until one spends from what one loves, directly testing attachment to acquired property. | terra: Attaining righteousness requires spending from what one loves, making release of valued possession rather than its retention the road to the good.

luna: The verse repeats that neither wealth nor children avail those who disbelieve, then names the Fire as their end; it is another direct formulation of the section’s warning. | terra: This repeated formula again denies that wealth or children can avail against God and names the fire as the abiding outcome.

luna: This verse praises those who spend in both ease and hardship. The section gives those same ease and hardship roots a financial sense, so the verse shows generosity across both fullness and want.

luna: The section’s b-kh-l means holding possessions back when they should be released; this verse describes those who withhold what Allah gave them, mistaking it for good, and says what they withheld will burden them on the Day of Resurrection. | terra: Those who are miserly with what God gave them mistake withholding for good, but the withheld gift becomes a collar around them on resurrection day.

luna: The section defines b-kh-l as keeping acquired property from where it should go; this verse names those who are stingy, urge others to stinginess, and conceal Allah’s bounty. | terra: This ayah condemns those who are miserly, command others to be miserly, and conceal the bounty God has given them, defining wealth as entrusted provision rather than self-sufficiency.
terra: Spending wealth merely to be seen by people is set against the section's giver who seeks God's face and no human repayment.
terra: If spouses separate, God can enrich each from His abundance, presenting sufficiency as His provision rather than possession of the other.
terra: All that is on earth, doubled, cannot ransom the rejecters from the day’s punishment, enlarging the failed purse to its conceivable maximum.
terra: The accusation that God's hand is chained is answered by His hands being outspread and His spending as He wills, opposing divine generosity to the closed-hand image of miserliness.
terra: Doors of plenty open after warning is forgotten, but seizure comes suddenly at the height of rejoicing, showing abundance unable to secure its possessors.

luna: The section’s image has property falling from its owner at death; here people arrive alone, having left what God provided behind, and their intercessors have disappeared. | terra: People come to God alone and leave behind everything He had conferred on them, making the death-bound loss of acquired possessions explicit.
terra: The Lord is the truly Rich and merciful and can remove one people and appoint successors, joining divine sufficiency to the fragility of human possession.
terra: At harvest, people must give the crop's due right; this directly answers the garden owners who try to exclude the poor from acquired produce.
terra: The people on the heights tell the arrogant that their gathered numbers or resources did not avail them, extending insufficiency beyond money to accumulated support.
terra: يُغْشِى ٱلَّيْلَ ٱلنَّهَارَ repeats the primary covering sense of 92:1, the physical image from which the section extends toward death's swoon.
terra: Adversity is replaced by prosperity until the people flourish, then sudden seizure breaks their confidence in continued ease.

luna: This verse likewise calls wealth and children a trial and says the great reward is with God. It gives another direct formulation of the section’s limit on treating possessions as personal sufficiency. | terra: Wealth and children are a trial while the great reward is with God, so abundance tests its holder rather than certifying success.
terra: Wealth spent to block God's path becomes regret and ends in defeat, showing that even expenditure cannot avail when directed toward the wrong end.
terra: Fear of poverty after excluding the idolaters is met with a promise that God can enrich from His bounty, moving security away from retained trade.

luna: This verse describes religious leaders who hoard gold and silver instead of spending in God’s way; it is a concrete form of the section’s miserly holding of possessions. | terra: Religious authorities who consume wealth wrongfully and hoard gold and silver instead of spending it enact the section's definition of withholding possessions from their due use.

luna: The next verse depicts that hoarded gold and silver heated and used to brand their foreheads, sides, and backs. It shows the hoarder’s wealth becoming punishment rather than protection. | terra: The hoard of 9:34 is heated in the fire and brands its owners, making retained wealth itself testify to its failure to protect them.

luna: The section says wealth cannot help at death; this verse says God means to punish disbelievers through their wealth and children in worldly life, while their souls depart in disbelief, reversing their apparent advantage. | terra: Wealth and children are not to impress: God makes them a means of torment in this life and their owners' souls depart in rejection.
terra: The people resented only after God and His messenger enriched them from divine bounty, locating their material sufficiency in a gift they then deny.
terra: They covenant that if God gives from His bounty they will give charity and become righteous, setting up the broken promise and miserliness exposed in 9:76.

luna: After receiving bounty, the people in this verse become miserly with it and turn away. This is the section’s movement from provision to withholding in an explicit narrative. | terra: After God gives them from His bounty, they بَخِلُوا۟ بِهِۦ and turn away, exactly joining acquired abundance, miserliness, and the section's turning-away stance.

luna: This verse similarly says God means to punish disbelievers through their wealth and children in worldly life, not grant security through them, giving the section’s insufficiency claim a sharp reversal. | terra: The warning repeats that wealth and children may become worldly torment and accompany no saving sufficiency at death.
terra: Charity is taken from their wealth to purify and increase them, matching the giver of 92:18 who gives his wealth seeking purification.
terra: God purchases believers' lives and wealth for the Garden, presenting surrendered possession as the exchange that endures.
terra: Worldly abundance is likened to flourishing vegetation whose owners think it under their control just before it is cut down, a direct nonlexical scene of plenty becoming nothing.
terra: Those who want worldly life and its adornment are paid their deeds in full within it, establishing a merely present and exhaustible return.
terra: The seekers of worldly return in 11:15 have only fire in the hereafter and find their works void, exposing the final insufficiency of that payment.
terra: Joseph's plan for seven years of abundant cultivation and stored grain gives a concrete scene of provision accumulated in anticipation of constriction.
terra: Seven severe years consume what was stored during the abundant years, staging the movement from fullness to hardship almost literally.
terra: A year of rain and pressing follows the famine, completing the scene with restored abundance after constriction.
terra: Jacob takes prudent measures for his sons yet states that he cannot avail them at all against God, marking the boundary of even parental protection.
terra: Joseph's brothers arrive under hardship with poor merchandise and ask for full measure and charity, placing generosity precisely at the meeting of need and limited means.
terra: The repeated phrase يُغْشِى ٱلَّيْلَ ٱلنَّهَارَ supplies another direct occurrence of night covering day.
terra: Those who reject their Lord would ransom themselves with everything on earth and as much again, but possession cannot discharge that reckoning.
terra: Those seeking their Lord's face spend secretly and openly from His provision, a close positive counterpart to giving without repayment.

luna: This verse says Allah expands and restricts provision, while people rejoice in worldly life. It joins the section’s financial reading of plenty and want to the warning that worldly abundance is limited. | terra: God expands and restricts provision, while people rejoice in a worldly life that is only a brief enjoyment beside the hereafter.
terra: The faithful must spend secretly and openly before a day with neither sale nor friendship, setting a deadline on wealth's useful release.
terra: At the destroyed people's fall, what they had earned did not avail them, a concise parallel to possessions failing at ruin.
terra: Those favored in provision refuse to pass it to people under their authority so that they might share equally, a social expression of treating provision as exclusively one's own.
terra: A powerless slave who owns nothing is contrasted with one given good provision who spends privately and publicly, joining possession, ability, and release in one parable.
terra: What people possess runs out, while what is with God remains; this is the clearest boundary between the held purse and lasting sufficiency.
terra: A town enjoying secure, abundant provision is made to taste hunger after ingratitude, staging a collective descent from ease to constriction.
terra: Giving the relative, poor person, and traveler their due treats part of one's possession as another's right rather than a private store.

luna: The section evokes the purse becoming full or empty and defines b-kh-l as holding possessions back; this verse pictures a hand neither chained to the neck nor extended completely, with destitution as the consequence of excess. | terra: The hand must be neither chained to the neck nor fully outspread; this bodily image sets a measured boundary between miserliness and ruinous expenditure.

luna: This verse says the Lord expands provision for whom He wills and restricts it. It makes financial plenty and shortage dependent on God rather than the holder’s self-sufficiency. | terra: God expands provision and measures it, grounding the spending measure in 17:29 in divine rather than self-made sufficiency.

luna: The section describes the wealthy miser as holding acquired possessions back; this verse says that if people owned the treasuries of their Lord’s mercy they would still withhold for fear of spending, naming the fear beneath grasping. | terra: Humans would withhold even the treasuries of divine mercy for fear that spending exhausts them, and the ayah names the human being as tightfisted.

luna: The owner of the two gardens boasts that he has more wealth and stronger support. His boast stages the section’s rich man who feels secure because of what he owns. | terra: The garden owner boasts that he has more wealth and a stronger following, giving narrative form to the self-sufficient stance.
terra: He enters his garden wronging himself and says it will never perish, transferring imagined personal sufficiency to his possessions.

luna: The garden owner says he does not think the Hour will come and expects something better if returned; this is self-sufficiency extended into a false promise of permanence, like the section’s warning about wealth at death. | terra: The garden owner expects both no Hour and a better resort if returned to his Lord, showing how wealth feeds confidence beyond death.
terra: The companion tells him to acknowledge God's will and power on entering the garden, correcting self-attribution while the property still stands.
terra: The companion warns that God may give him something better and strike the boastful man's garden, making both increase and loss God's disposal.
terra: The warning that the garden's water may sink beyond recovery supplies the concrete means by which apparent abundance can empty.

luna: After his gardens are ruined, the owner wrings his hands over what he spent. The scene makes visible the section’s claim that accumulated wealth can slip away and leave its owner helpless. | terra: When his produce is destroyed, he wrings his hands over what he spent on it; abundance has become empty-handed loss in a single scene.

luna: The garden owner has no group to help him against God. This is the story’s explicit answer to the security implied by his wealth and status. | terra: After the garden falls, no party can help him besides God and he cannot help himself, marking the exact limit of possessions and social strength.
luna: The story concludes that true protection belongs to God, the Real; this supplies the source of lasting help after the wealthy owner’s possessions and human backing fail.
terra: The parable immediately before 18:46 makes worldly life vegetation that flourishes with rain and then becomes wind-scattered debris.

luna: This verse calls wealth and children adornment of worldly life and says enduring good deeds are better. It gives a specific account of what lasts after the section’s possessions have failed. | terra: Wealth and children are worldly adornment, whereas enduring good deeds are better in reward and hope; the ayah distinguishes what is held briefly from what remains.
terra: Moses asks not to be burdened with difficulty because of forgetfulness; this preserves the ʿusr root's ordinary sense outside the section's financial extension.
terra: The righteous person is promised the finest reward and an easy command, another moral setting in which ease is divinely directed.
terra: God inherits the earth and everyone upon it, supplying the ultimate ownership behind each person's abandonment of acquired goods.
terra: A rejecter confidently claims that he will be given wealth and children, voicing the presumption that possession continues beyond accountability.
terra: God inherits what the man claims in 19:77, and the man comes alone; the promised possessions pass away from their claimant.

luna: The section names r-d-y as ruin and links it to the moment when wealth cannot help; here Moses is warned not to follow desire and perish, giving the same root a moral downfall sense connected to turning away. | terra: فَتَرْدَىٰ uses the same ruin root as 92:11: denial of the Hour and preference following desire end in perishing.
luna: The section names the root gh-sh-w for covering and gives death-swoon as a secondary sense; here the sea covers Pharaoh’s people in a fatal scene, a concrete lethal form of that covering.
terra: The addressee must not strain toward others' worldly splendor; the Lord's provision is better and more enduring.
terra: The question asks whether the wealth and sons supplied to people are being mistaken for a hastening of good things.
terra: The answer denies the inference in 23:55: abundant provision is not itself proof of good or favor.

luna: The section says the miser’s money cannot help once he falls; this verse gives the dying person’s plea to return and act, a final boundary on the time left for giving. | terra: At death the person asks to be sent back, closely paralleling the request for postponement in 63:10.

luna: The next verse says a barrier lies behind the dead until resurrection. It completes the return-request scene by closing the chance to act again. | terra: He wants to do good in what he left behind, but a barrier prevents return; the unspent opportunity cannot be recovered after death.
terra: People of means must not swear to stop giving relatives, the needy, and emigrants; pardon replaces the impulse to close the purse after injury.
terra: If prospective spouses are poor, God will enrich them from His bounty; poverty is a condition He can change, not a final measure of worth.
terra: Owners are told to give contracted slaves from the wealth God gave them, defining property as divine provision containing another person's route to freedom.

luna: The section names stinginess as holding possessions back and generosity as its opposite; this verse describes spending without extravagance or miserliness, giving a measured practice between closed and emptied hands. | terra: The servants' spending is neither extravagant nor miserly but measured between them, giving the behavioral balance absent from the self-sufficient hoarder.

luna: The section invokes Abraham’s prayer for the Day when neither wealth nor sons benefit (la yanfa‘u malun wa la banun). This is the direct limit on the assets the miser counts on. | terra: يَوْمَ لَا يَنفَعُ مَالٌ وَلَا بَنُونَ states the same boundary as 92:11 at the judgment scene: neither wealth nor children benefit.

luna: After 26:88 says wealth and sons do not benefit on that Day, this verse names the sound heart as the exception, specifying what has value when possessions fail. | terra: After 26:88 strips wealth and children of benefit, this ayah names the sound heart as what can meet God safely.
terra: Long enjoyment does not avail people when the threatened punishment comes, extending the section's question from money to every benefit enjoyed before the fall.
terra: Solomon says gratitude benefits the grateful person, while his Lord is truly Rich and Generous, relocating sufficiency from the receiver of treasure to its giver.
terra: Whatever people are given is temporary worldly enjoyment and adornment, while what is with God is better and more lasting.

luna: Qarun is given treasures so abundant that their keys burden a group of strong men. This makes the section’s full purse concrete before the story shows what that wealth can and cannot do. | terra: Qarun's treasure is so abundant that even its keys burden a company, establishing the scale of possession that still cannot prevent his fall.
terra: Qarun is told to seek the hereafter with what God gave him and to do good, identifying the use that could have made wealth serve rather than deceive.

luna: The section’s istaghna describes imagined self-sufficiency; Qarun says his wealth was given because of knowledge he possesses, presenting the same claim of standing secure through oneself. | terra: Qarun attributes his fortune to knowledge he possesses, a narrative instance of treating acquired wealth as self-sufficiency.

luna: Qarun comes before his people in his adornment, and those who desire worldly life wish for his position. This shows wealth’s public power before the section’s warning that it cannot secure its owner. | terra: Those dazzled by worldly life wish for Qarun's fortune, showing the social appeal of reading visible abundance as success.

luna: The knowledgeable observers say God’s reward is better for the one who believes and acts well. Their response sets durable worth against the wealth and display that attract the crowd in the preceding verse. | terra: People of knowledge answer that God's reward is better for faith and right action, supplying the counter-measure to Qarun's display.

luna: The earth swallows Qarun and his house, and he has no group to help him. This is a precise reversal of the rich man’s apparent security: his property and status cannot protect him. | terra: God makes the earth swallow Qarun and his house; neither his faction nor he can save him, vividly staging the fall at which accumulated wealth cannot avail.

luna: After Qarun’s fall, the people who wanted his position recognize that God expands and restricts provision as He wills. This directly joins the section’s wealth-and-want reading to the collapse of presumed self-sufficiency. | terra: Those who had desired Qarun's place now recognize that God expands and restricts provision, correcting their reading of abundance after his fall.
terra: Creatures that do not carry their own provision are still provided for by God, countering the fear that security depends upon hoarding a store.
terra: God expands provision for whom He wills and measures it, repeating the section's abundance-constriction relation.
terra: The question reminds people that God expands provision and restricts it, another direct formulation of the purse's fullness and emptiness under His measure.
terra: The command to give relatives, the poor, and travelers their due is explicitly for those seeking God's face, meeting both rightful release and pure motive.

luna: This verse distinguishes wealth given to increase through people’s property from charity seeking God’s face; it clarifies the section’s giver who expects no payment from a human recipient. | terra: An increase sought through other people's wealth does not increase with God, whereas zakat given seeking God's face is multiplied; this directly tests what gain and repayment mean.

luna: The section develops the root gh-sh-w as covering and links it to death-swoon; here waves cover people like canopies and they call to God in helplessness, a parallel of exposure to what overwhelms them.

luna: The section’s j-z-y dictionary note gives “a father cannot repay for his child” as an example; this verse states that on the Day of Judgment neither parent nor child can avail the other, making that exact limit explicit in its own warning about the Day. | terra: لَا يَجْزِي وَالِدٌ عَن وَلَدِهِ gives the section's dictionary example of jazāʾ as being enough for another, then denies that sufficiency in both parent-child directions on the promised day.
terra: The ayah remarkably joins stinginess with the section's secondary death sense: أَشِحَّةً عَلَيْكُمْ and the gaze of one يُغْشَىٰ عَلَيْهِ مِنَ ٱلْمَوْتِ.
terra: The people of Saba receive two gardens and are told to eat their Lord's provision gratefully, establishing conspicuous abundance as a gift.
terra: When they turn away, the flood replaces the fruitful gardens with bitter growth, a collective movement from plenty to deprivation.
terra: Their loss is named as recompense for ingratitude, giving the abundance-to-hardship reversal its moral relation.

luna: The people claim that their greater wealth and children will spare them from punishment. This is a specific claim of material security that 34:37 directly answers. | terra: The affluent claim that greater wealth and more children mean they will not be punished, stating the false immunity that 92:11 denies.

luna: This verse says Allah expands and restricts provision as He wills. It gives the section’s abundance-and-lack image a direct statement that provision is not controlled by the wealthy person. | terra: God expands and restricts provision, directly correcting the affluent boast in 34:35 that quantity of wealth proves immunity.

luna: The verse says wealth and children do not bring people near to God, except faith and righteous action. It directly denies that possessions create the sufficiency the section attributes to the miser’s self-image. | terra: Wealth and children do not bring a person near to God; faith and right action supply the different measure and multiplied reward.

luna: This verse says what people spend is replaced by God. That offers a specific counterpart to the section’s giver, who seeks God’s face rather than asking a person to repay him. | terra: God expands or restricts provision and replaces whatever is spent, answering the fear that released wealth leaves only lack.

luna: The verse says people are the poor toward Allah and Allah is al-Ghani. This repeats the section’s contrast between human need and the true source of sufficiency. | terra: Humans are the poor in need of God, while God alone is the Rich and Praiseworthy; this directly relocates true sufficiency.
terra: Those who spend secretly and openly hope for a commerce that will never perish, a deliberate alternative to the perishing commerce of accumulated wealth.
terra: God pays their rewards in full and adds from His bounty, completing the imperishable commerce of 35:29 with true sufficiency and recompense.
terra: When commanded to spend from God's provision, the rejecters refuse to feed those in need and use providence itself as their excuse for withholding.
terra: The sudden blast leaves people unable to make a bequest or return to their families, fixing the instant at which control of property and household ends.
terra: A saved speaker tells his former companion إِن كِدتَّ لَتُرْدِينِ, preserving the root's causative sense of bringing someone to ruin.
terra: Even all earthly wealth doubled would be offered to escape the evil of judgment, making the wished-for payment explicitly insufficient.
terra: When hardship touches a person he calls on God, but after a blessing he claims it came through his own knowledge, reenacting the move from need to self-sufficiency.
terra: Those before made the same claim, but what they had earned did not avail them, answering self-attribution with failed acquisition.
terra: The passage closes by asking whether they know that God expands and restricts provision, naming the true source of both states.
terra: Destroyed peoples possessed greater strength and آثار, yet what they earned did not avail them when judgment arrived.

luna: After hardship is removed and blessing arrives, the person says “this is mine” and doubts the Hour. This is a specific case of ease becoming an assertion of security, like the section’s self-sufficient man. | terra: After mercy following hardship, a person calls it his own and expects the best even if returned to God, a clear self-sufficient reading of restored abundance.
terra: When blessed, the person turns away, but adversity makes him pray at length; the two states expose the instability of his claimed independence.
terra: The keys of heaven and earth belong to God, who expands and restricts provision; ownership and its changing measure meet in one formulation.
terra: The person seeking the hereafter's harvest receives increase, while the seeker of the worldly harvest gets only some of it and no share in the hereafter.
terra: If provision were expanded without measure, people would transgress; God sends it in due measure, joining abundance to the danger named in 96:6-7.
terra: God apportions livelihoods and raises some over others in degree, while His mercy is better than what people accumulate.
terra: The ayah imagines roofs and stairways of silver for rejecters, beginning a deliberate devaluation of visible wealth.
terra: Gold and luxury are called only enjoyment of worldly life, whereas the hereafter with the Lord belongs to the God-fearing.
terra: The people leave behind gardens and springs at destruction, showing that possessed abundance does not accompany its holders.
terra: Comforts in which they delighted are included among what is abandoned.
terra: God makes another people inherit those goods, completing the transfer that empties ownership at the former holders' fall.
terra: On the decisive day no protector or relation can avail another and none are helped, another interpersonal boundary on compensating for someone else.
terra: Neither what the condemned earned nor their protectors avail them against the waiting fire, closely matching wealth's failure at ruin.
terra: The condemned are told that they exhausted their good things in worldly life and enjoyed them there, leaving humiliation when that enjoyment ends.
terra: نَظَرَ ٱلْمَغْشِىِّ عَلَيْهِ مِنَ ٱلْمَوْتِ is the Quranic death-swoon wording that realizes the section's dictionary extension from night covering to death covering a person.
terra: The preceding question to 47:38 says that if God pressed people for their wealth they would become miserly, exposing what their attachment to possession contains.

luna: The section links b-kh-l (withholding possessions) with gh-n-y (self-sufficiency). This verse joins the same root b-kh-l to “Allah is al-Ghani and you are poor,” overturning the miser’s claim to sufficiency. | terra: The ayah joins miserliness and turning away, then corrects imagined self-sufficiency with وَٱللَّهُ ٱلْغَنِىُّ وَأَنتُمُ ٱلْفُقَرَآءُ: God is rich and humans are needy.

luna: The verse names the stupor of death arriving with truth. The section’s dictionary explicitly gives death-swoon as a secondary sense of the root behind 92:1’s covering, and places the loss of wealth at that threshold. | terra: The stupor of death arrives with the truth one tried to evade, a direct nonlexical realization of the section's gloss about death's covering faintness.

luna: The section defines withholding as keeping possessions from their proper recipient; this verse says there is a recognized right in wealth for the asker and deprived person, the direct claim that wealth is not only for its holder. | terra: A recognized right for the asker and deprived person exists within their wealth, directly specifying what must not be withheld from its claimant.
terra: God asks no provision from people and does not ask them to feed Him, clarifying that human giving can never be repayment of a divine need.
terra: God alone is the Provider and possessor of firm strength, completing 51:57's denial that He needs what humans hold.
terra: Each person's own striving is recompensed with the fullest recompense, helping distinguish divine repayment from giving in order to settle a human favor.
terra: وَأَنَّهُۥ هُوَ أَغْنَىٰ وَأَقْنَىٰ attributes both enrichment and the giving of holdings to God; أَقْنَىٰ also meets the source section's qinyah language for acquired property.

luna: This verse stages the soul reaching the throat while onlookers watch; it gives bodily form to the death threshold at which the section says possessions slip from their owner. | terra: The soul reaching the throat presents the same death threshold at which material sufficiency ends.

luna: The verse describes the onlookers standing nearby as the soul reaches the throat, completing the helpless scene at which the section’s wealth can no longer suffice. | terra: Those present can only watch the dying person, unable to make their resources sufficient for him.
luna: The verse says Allah is nearer to the dying person than the observers, though they do not perceive it. This places divine reality beyond the visible wealth left around the deathbed.
luna: At the moment the soul reaches the throat, this verse challenges the living to return it if they can. Its context makes explicit the helplessness behind the section’s deathbed image.

luna: The passage concludes by challenging the onlookers to bring the soul back if they are truthful; this completes the helpless death scene behind the section’s image of wealth dropping away. | terra: The challenge to return the soul, if humans are truly unaccountable, makes their inability at death the test of claimed independence.
terra: People must spend from what God has made them successors over, explicitly describing wealth as temporary custody rather than independent possession.
terra: The question why people do not spend is answered by God's inheritance of heaven and earth, exposing every human holding as temporary custody.
terra: A good loan to God is multiplied and receives a noble reward, answering the fear that generosity only empties the hand.
terra: Charitable men and women are described as lending God a good loan that is multiplied, relocating adequate repayment from recipient to Lord.

luna: This verse describes worldly life as rivalry in increase of wealth and children, then as growth that withers and becomes debris. The passing sequence illuminates the section’s image of possessions slipping away. | terra: Worldly rivalry in wealth and children is compared to growth that pleases and then withers into debris, showing acquired abundance passing away.
terra: People are told neither to grieve over what escapes them nor exult in what arrives, preparing the diagnosis of proud miserliness in 57:24.

luna: The section’s image centers on b-kh-l and presumed self-sufficiency; this verse names the stingy person who commands stinginess and says Allah is al-Ghani, worthy of praise. | terra: Those who are miserly and command miserliness are answered with God's independence, so withholding harms no need in God and reveals only the holder's mistake.

luna: This verse says neither wealth nor children will avail against God and names their owners as companions of the Fire, a direct parallel to the section’s limit on wealth. | terra: Neither wealth nor children can avail their owners against God here; the ayah makes the same possessions that signify abundance powerless before the fire.
terra: The distribution rule prevents wealth from circulating only among the rich, making the social release of possessions an explicit boundary on accumulation.

luna: The section presents b-kh-l as the miser’s path; this verse praises people who prefer others over themselves even when they themselves are in need and says those protected from their own avarice succeed. | terra: The Helpers prefer others even while in privation, and success belongs to those protected from their own stinginess; need here becomes the setting for generosity.

luna: The verse says kin and children will not benefit on the Day of Resurrection and that God sees what people do. It extends the section’s boundary from wealth to family ties. | terra: Neither relatives nor children benefit people on resurrection day, extending the insufficiency of possessions to the closest human bonds.
terra: The offer of a commerce that saves from painful punishment introduces the enduring exchange whose price in 61:11 includes wealth.
terra: The saving commerce of 61:10 consists in faith and striving with wealth and life, showing the use through which wealth can serve beyond death.
terra: People leave the sermon for trade or amusement, but what is with God is better and God is the best provider.

luna: This verse warns believers not to let wealth and children distract them from remembering Allah, because those who do are losers. It shows wealth failing as a guide to what matters. | terra: Wealth and children must not distract from God's remembrance; those so distracted are named the losers before the death-regret scene of 63:10.

luna: At death, a person asks for a brief delay so he can give charity (fa-assaddaqa). This directly matches the section’s scene of wealth no longer helping at the fall and the dying person wishing he had given. | terra: At death's approach the holder of provision asks for a brief delay specifically so that he may give charity, staging the section's claim that wealth becomes useful only by being released before the fall.

luna: After the dying person asks in 63:10 for time to give charity, this neighboring verse says Allah will not delay a soul when its term arrives. It closes the scene of too-late regret. | terra: God will not delay a soul once its term comes, closing the extension requested for charitable giving in 63:10.

luna: This verse calls wealth and children a trial and says great reward is with God. The following verse commands spending and guarding against the soul’s avarice, completing the contrast between possessions as a test and what brings success. | terra: Wealth and children are a trial, while immense reward is with God; this distinguishes possessed means from the final measure.

luna: This verse commands spending and says whoever is protected from the avarice of his own soul succeeds, directly naming the inward counterpart of the section’s b-kh-l. | terra: The command to spend for one's own good and the promise of success to those protected from inner stinginess reverse the miser's claim that retaining wealth serves him.
terra: A good loan to God is multiplied and forgiven, so expenditure leads to divine increase rather than the loss feared by miserliness.

luna: The section reads al-yusr and al-‘usr through wealth and want; this verse explicitly joins spending according to one’s sa‘a (means) to Allah making ease after ‘usr, showing both its financial and ordinary sense. | terra: The wealthy person must spend from his abundance, the constrained from what God gave him, and the ayah closes with God's promise to place ease after hardship.
terra: The husbands of Noah's and Lot's wives cannot avail them against God, a concrete relational instance of one person being unable to suffice for another.
terra: The ayah asks who could provide if God withheld His provision, exposing the dependence hidden by apparent self-sufficiency.
terra: The garden owners are tested through property they assume they can harvest on their own terms, opening a scene of possession and withheld giving.
terra: They make their plan without reservation, showing the confidence in continued possession that the night's destruction will undo.
terra: A visitation from the Lord passes over the garden while they sleep, making loss arrive beneath the cover of night.
terra: By morning the abundant garden has become stripped and dark, a literal passage from means to deprivation.
terra: Their whispered order that no poor person enter the garden that day states the intended withholding of the poor person's share.
terra: They go out resolved and believing themselves able to exclude, joining miserliness to imagined control over the crop.
terra: On seeing the ruined garden they first think they have lost the way, registering how completely possession has vanished.
terra: They finally say that they have been deprived, reversing their plan to deprive the poor person in 68:24.
terra: After acknowledging wrongdoing, the garden owners hope their Lord will replace the lost garden with something better, relocating future means in God.
terra: The passage identifies the garden's destruction as punishment and points to a greater hereafter punishment, preventing the material loss from being read as merely accidental.

luna: The section quotes this exact lament by the person given his record in his left hand: “my wealth did not avail me” (ma aghna ‘anni maliyah), a direct boundary on what possessions can save. | terra: The condemned person says مَا أَغْنَىٰ عَنِّى مَالِيَهْ in his own voice, turning the section's claim that wealth will not suffice into a confession after judgment.

luna: After the speaker says in 69:28 that his wealth did not avail him, this verse says his authority has perished too. It completes the loss of the resources he might have counted on. | terra: Immediately after the confession that wealth did not avail, the speaker says his authority has perished too, extending insufficiency from property to power.
terra: At judgment the criminal wishes to ransom himself with his own children, a direct family form of the compensation that cannot suffice.
terra: The wished-for ransom expands from children to spouse and brother, showing intimate relationships treated as payments that still cannot save.
terra: He would offer everyone on earth if it could save him, expanding the failed ransom to the largest imaginable worldly possession.
terra: The blaze calls the person who turned away; with 70:18 it joins the turning-away figure of surah 92 to gathered, hoarded wealth.
terra: جَمَعَ فَأَوْعَىٰ depicts the one who gathers and stores away, the clearest nonlexical parallel to holding acquired goods back.

luna: This verse says the human being is distressed when touched by hardship; it supplies the shortage side of the next verse’s response to abundance. | terra: Human anxiety under harm precedes the withholding response to received good in 70:21, joining fear of constriction to the closed hand.
luna: The next verse says that when good reaches the human being, he withholds (manu‘a). It directly joins prosperity to the grasping conduct developed in the section.

luna: The section frames wealth as possessions that can be held or released; this verse says the steadfast worshippers reserve a recognized share of their wealth for others. | terra: The worshippers' wealth contains a known right, defining property as carrying an obligation rather than conferring independence.

luna: This verse identifies the recipients of that share as the asker and the deprived, giving a concrete opposite to the section’s miser who keeps wealth back. | terra: This ayah names the asker and the deprived person as the recipients of the known right in 70:24.
terra: Noah's people follow one whose wealth and children increase him only in loss, reversing abundance into spiritual deficit.
terra: The command to give God a good loan and send good ahead promises that it will be found with God better and greater in reward.

luna: The section says the giver does not give to settle a debt or receive recompense; this command warns against giving in order to get more in return (wa la تمنن تستكثر), a direct boundary on transactional generosity. | terra: وَلَا تَمْنُن تَسْتَكْثِرُ forbids giving a favor in order to obtain more, sharply defining the non-transactional giving described in the section.
luna: The section’s root ‘-s-r names both financial shortage and hardship; this verse uses its “difficult” form for the Day the Trumpet is blown, extending the word’s hardship sense to judgment.
luna: The section glosses ‘-s-r through want and difficulty; this verse says that Day will not be easy for disbelievers, joining the same ease/difficulty axis to the fate beyond worldly wealth.
terra: The condemned man is given extensive wealth, establishing the abundance that feeds his later demand for still more.
terra: God says He made the man's worldly circumstances smooth and ample, supplying the ease from which the man's unsatisfied desire for increase in 74:15 arises.
terra: Despite extensive wealth and an eased life, he greedily desires an increase, showing that abundance has not made him inwardly sufficient.

luna: This verse stages the death moment as the soul reaching the collarbones. The section’s dictionary connects 92:1’s covering root to death-swoon, and says the owner’s wealth fails at that threshold. | terra: The soul reaching the collarbones marks the bodily threshold at which the section says held wealth slips from the hand.

luna: As the death scene continues, those present ask who can heal the dying person. This shows the limit of human help at the point where the section says possessions can no longer suffice. | terra: The cry for someone to cure the dying person exposes the limits of every available means at that threshold.

luna: The dying person recognizes that this is departure, completing the scene of the section’s death threshold where held wealth slips away. | terra: The dying person realizes that separation has arrived, giving awareness to the moment of irreversible loss.
luna: The verse describes the legs being joined together as death approaches; it continues the bodily scene of the final moment that the section associates with loss of possessions.

luna: The passage ends with the person being driven to his Lord. This completes the death scene and turns from possessions that cannot help to the reckoning that follows. | terra: The person is driven to the Lord, locating final ownership and destination beyond the possessions now left behind.

luna: The section’s giver releases what he owns without seeking a return; this verse depicts people giving food to the poor, orphan, and captive. The next verse states their motive, but this verse contributes the concrete act of giving. | terra: They give food they themselves value to the needy, orphan, and captive; 76:9 then discloses a motive free of repayment or thanks.

luna: The section says the giver seeks God’s face and expects no repayment from anyone; here the people who feed others say they want from them neither recompense nor thanks (la nuridu minkum jaz’an wa la shukura). | terra: The givers say they feed only for God's face and want neither جَزَآءً nor thanks, an explicit counterpart to giving without a favor to be repaid.

luna: This is the frown and turning away that begins the passage cited by the section; the following verses identify the visitor as blind, so this row opens the scene in which attention shifts toward the self-sufficient man.
luna: This verse identifies the visitor as the blind man, completing the scene behind the section’s contrast between the man who sees himself as sufficient and the seeker who came for guidance.
luna: The rebuke asks what could make the Prophet know that the blind visitor might be purified. It explains why the neglected seeker mattered in the scene cited by the section.
luna: The verse says the blind visitor might receive a reminder and benefit; it shows the value of the seeker whom the self-satisfied visitor displaced.

luna: The section cites this exact istaghna form for the person who considers himself sufficient, in contrast to the miser’s path in 92:8; here the Prophet is drawn toward the self-satisfied visitor. | terra: أَمَّا مَنِ ٱسْتَغْنَىٰ identifies the self-sufficient-seeming man in the very encounter developed by the section.

luna: The section says the self-sufficient man receives attention; this is the rebuke’s next detail, “you attend to him” (tasadda), while the blind seeker is neglected in the surrounding passage. | terra: This ayah supplies the response to 80:5: the Prophet directs his attention to the man who presents himself as self-sufficient.

luna: The section describes attention given to the self-sufficient man; this verse says the Prophet is not accountable if that man does not purify himself, clarifying the misplaced priority in the rebuke. | terra: The warning says the addressee is not accountable for whether the self-sufficient man purifies himself, qualifying the attention given him in 80:6.

luna: The passage turns from the self-satisfied man to one who comes striving; this neighboring contrast gives the neglected seeker’s own approach. | terra: The other man comes actively seeking, beginning the human contrast to the one who presents himself as self-sufficient.

luna: The seeker is described as fearing God, completing the contrast with the man who considers himself self-sufficient in the section’s cited passage. | terra: The seeker fears God, the stance opposite to self-sufficiency that explains why his approach matters.

luna: The passage says the Prophet is distracted from this God-fearing seeker. It completes the rebuke’s reversal of attention around self-sufficiency and need. | terra: The Prophet's distraction from the fearful seeker completes the reversal for which attention to the self-sufficient man is corrected.
terra: No soul possesses anything for another on that day and all command belongs to God, expressing the same failed interpersonal sufficiency without relying on wealth.

luna: The section names al-yusra in 92:7 and traces it to y-s-r; here Allah says He will ease the Prophet toward al-yusra, a close wording in a different, nonfinancial setting. | terra: وَنُيَسِّرُكَ لِلْيُسْرَىٰ closely echoes the promise of being eased toward ease and preserves its directed, divinely enabled sense outside surah 92.
terra: Preferring the nearer life states the choice that makes worldly holdings appear sufficient.
terra: The hereafter is better and more enduring, supplying the lasting side of the contrast to 87:16.
terra: The food of hell neither nourishes nor avails against hunger, giving the section's 'does not suffice' sense a concrete and terrible object.

luna: The section reads ease and hardship as abundance and lack. Here a person interprets expanded provision as proof that God honored him; the following verses expose that inference as false. | terra: A human reads generous provision as proof that his Lord has honored him, exposing the mistaken equation between abundance and worth.

luna: The section’s financial reading of ease and hardship meets this verse’s restricted provision, which the person wrongly treats as humiliation. Its own claim supplies the scarcity side of that mistaken equation. | terra: When provision is measured tightly, the same person calls it humiliation; together with 89:15 this names the false moral reading of fullness and emptiness.

luna: After the rich person’s mistaken inference, this verse says they do not honor the orphan; abundance has not made the holder generous, directly exposing the section’s b-kh-l pattern. | terra: The correction begins by saying they do not honor the orphan, shifting the measure of honor from received wealth to its treatment of the vulnerable.

luna: This verse says they do not urge feeding the poor. It gives a concrete human cost for the section’s image of holding acquired wealth instead of letting it benefit others. | terra: Failure to urge feeding the poor shows the withholding concealed behind the complaints about constricted provision.

luna: The section glosses wealth as acquired possessions and stinginess as keeping them back; this verse depicts devouring inheritance greedily, a particularly direct form of grasping at property. | terra: Consuming inheritance greedily depicts acquisition without regard for another's due share.

luna: The section’s image of a man rich in possessions who sees himself as sufficient is sharpened here by the claim that people love wealth with an intense love. | terra: An excessive love of wealth names the attachment that makes possession feel like sufficiency and giving feel like loss.
terra: After the passage exposes greed for wealth, hell is brought near and the human being finally remembers at judgment.
terra: The person wishes he had sent something ahead for his life, reversing the earlier habit of consuming and retaining into too-late recognition.
terra: The boast that one has consumed abundant wealth makes the amount spent a claim of status, immediately before the surah tests whether he took the steep path of liberating and feeding.
terra: The person has not attempted the steep path, introducing moral difficulty as the route the possessor avoids.
terra: Freeing a slave defines the steep path of 90:11 through costly release rather than acquisition.
terra: Feeding on a day of hunger makes material constriction the very occasion for generous action.
terra: The orphaned relative is one concrete recipient of the difficult generosity named by the passage.
terra: The destitute person in misery is the other recipient, placing the giver beside the person at the extreme of empty-handed need.

luna: The section develops yaghsha in 92:1 as night covering a person, with a dictionary sense extending to death-swoon; 91:4 repeats the night-covering scene (yaghshaha), though its referent is the celestial body in the surrounding oath.

luna: The section notes that the next surah says Allah found the Prophet in need and enriched him (a’ila fa-agna). It makes sufficiency a gift from God rather than an achievement secured by hoarded property. | terra: وَوَجَدَكَ عَآئِلًا فَأَغْنَىٰ assigns enrichment to God and reverses the self-produced sufficiency imagined in ٱسْتَغْنَىٰ.
terra: Following God's enrichment in 93:8, the addressee must not oppress the orphan; received abundance is converted into responsibility.
terra: Following God's enrichment in 93:8, the beggar must not be repelled, reversing the closed hand of the self-sufficient person.

luna: The section reads the ‘-s-r/y-s-r pair financially; this verse uses ‘usr for difficulty and yusr for ease in the repeated promise that ease accompanies hardship, without making the subject money. | terra: فَإِنَّ مَعَ ٱلْعُسْرِ يُسْرًا places ease with hardship and supplies the plain semantic axis that the section hears again as wealth and poverty.

luna: This repeats the section’s named ‘-s-r/y-s-r roots in the ordinary sense of hardship and ease. The repetition strengthens the other, financial sense developed in the section. | terra: The repeated promise that ease is with hardship reinforces the axis rather than treating hardship as the final condition.

luna: The section’s source word istaghna in 92:8 means that a person sees himself as self-sufficient; 96:6 says the human being transgresses, setting up the consequence of that stance. | terra: This ayah gives the consequence completed by 96:7: the human being transgresses when he sees himself as self-sufficient.

luna: The section’s source word istaghna in 92:8 means seeing oneself as sufficient; this verse names precisely that trigger, “when he sees himself as self-sufficient” (ra’ahu istaghna). | terra: أَن رَّآهُ ٱسْتَغْنَىٰ names exactly the self-perception of sufficiency carried by the miser in 92:8.

luna: This verse says a person loves wealth intensely. It repeats the section’s specific image of attachment to possessions, also stated in 89:20, and explains the inward pull behind withholding them. | terra: The human being's intense love of wealth identifies the attachment behind counting, withholding, and imagined self-sufficiency.
terra: The graves being overturned sets the judgment boundary immediately after 100:8's love of wealth.
terra: Competition for increase distracts people, naming accumulation itself as the activity that masks its insufficiency.
terra: The distraction of accumulation lasts until people reach the graves, placing its limit at precisely the death threshold developed in the section.
terra: People will be questioned that day about their enjoyed abundance, making worldly comfort an accountable trust rather than self-validating wealth.

luna: This verse describes gathering wealth and counting it; the next verse says the collector imagines his wealth will make him immortal, the exact false security the section sets beside death. | terra: ٱلَّذِى جَمَعَ مَالًا وَعَدَّدَهُ depicts wealth gathered and repeatedly counted, the possessed store on which false sufficiency rests.

luna: The section names the belief that wealth can secure permanence; this verse says the collector imagines his wealth will make him immortal (akhla-dahu), exposing that false sufficiency. | terra: The accumulator thinks his wealth has made him immortal, stating the precise illusion that money can survive or prevent the moment in 92:11.

luna: After 104:2-3 depicts wealth amassed and imagined to grant permanence, this verse says the person will be cast into al-Hutama, showing the limit of that imagined security. | terra: كَلَّا لَيُنۢبَذَنَّ فِى ٱلْحُطَمَةِ breaks the immortality calculation of 104:3 by showing the hoarder cast into the Crusher.
terra: Failure to urge feeding the poor is a direct social form of retaining provision instead of directing it to need.
terra: Withholding even ordinary aid is the small-scale form of keeping possessions from those to whom access should not be denied.

luna: The section explicitly compares 92:11 with this sentence about Abu Lahab: his wealth did not avail him (ma aghna ‘anhu maluhu). The wording makes the failure of material sufficiency unmistakable. | terra: Its near-verbatim مَا أَغْنَىٰ عَنْهُ مَالُهُ states the section's knot directly: acquired wealth cannot suffice when ruin arrives.

luna: The section cites 111:2’s statement that Abu Lahab’s wealth and earnings did not avail him; this next verse names the blazing fire he will enter, giving the failure its immediate consequence. | terra: Immediately after 111:2 says wealth did not avail Abu Lahab, this ayah supplies the consequence: entry into a flaming fire.
